clue.text: A little bit cut from start of unpleasant film after one PM in India

indicators.note: a film cut from its start loses its opening, so the word loses its first letter
'after' as sequence: the film chunk comes after the PM

parts.note: SCUM, a nasty film on a surface, losing its first letter

explanation.surface: A censor snips a bit from the opening of a nasty film once the Indian prime minister has had a look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' pretends to be cinema; it is the skin of scum on a pond. 'One PM' is a person, not a time of day.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: modicum is a small quantity, usually heard in 'a modicum of sense'.

clue.text: It's difficult having Scottish island seafood filleted

indicators.note: filleting takes the backbone out of the middle of a fish, so the middle LF goes

parts.note: MULL, an island of the Inner Hebrides, its last L lost in the filleting
FISH, its F lost in the filleting

explanation.surface: A complaint that Scottish island fish is hard work once it has been filleted.
explanation.walkthrough: MULL FISH strung together is 'filleted': its middle, LF, is taken out like a backbone.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubborn as a mule, and a stubborn person is difficult to deal with.

clue.text: Narcos got head of family of 4. That's absolutely right!

parts.note: narcs, US narcotics agents, work for the Drug Enforcement Administration
4 down is MAFIA, and a mafia family is headed by a don

explanation.surface: A gangster film line: the drug squad finally caught the mob boss, and everyone agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Narcos' reads as the drug dealers; here it is the agents chasing them. 'Got' only joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: something exactly on target is spot on, so saying it agrees that a thing is absolutely right.

clue.text: How did Cane make ane mickle pickle?

parts.note: a cane is a stick; compare CANE with ANE and see which letter departed
Scots: ane = one, mickle = big, so 'one big pickle', a predicament

explanation.surface: A Scots riddle about how a word lost its first letter and got into a big mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as three words, C LEFT STICK: that is how CANE became ANE. 'Ane' and 'mickle' are Scots for 'one' and 'large'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a split stick pins whatever is caught in it, so being in one means being stuck in a pickle.

clue.text: Mob. 1-1-0-1000 dialled up

indicators.note: 'up' in a down clue sends the letters upward, reading bottom to top; 'dialled' suits numbers you ring

parts.note: FA, as in 'sweet FA' (sweet Fanny Adams), means nothing

explanation.surface: A phone number for the mob, dialled in.
explanation.walkthrough: The digits look like a phone number; each stands for letters instead. Sweet FA is British slang for nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the Sicilian crime syndicate is the archetypal gang, and organised criminals are called the mob.

clue.text: Math in Cambridge University one's caught copying

parts.note: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in Cambridge, Massachusetts
the setter, Math, refers to himself
c = caught, the cricket scorecard abbreviation

explanation.surface: The setter, a student at Cambridge, has been caught cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridge is the one in Massachusetts, not England. 'Math' is the setter's pseudonym, so it gives ME, not a school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: from Greek mimesis, it describes imitation, as mimicry does.

clue.text: Dude! Please leave some vegetables!

parts.note: 'Man!' and 'Dude!' are both casual forms of address

explanation.surface: Someone begs a greedy friend not to eat all the vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for vegetables to be left on the plate; the wordplay tells a person to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: French for 'eat all', as the pod is eaten whole; the word is its own plural, hence 'some'.

clue.text: Seemingly hungry chap gives a whimper!

indicators.note: a hungry person seems to have an empty stomach

parts.note: an empty belly: O, nothing, in the middle

explanation.surface: A hungry man whimpers.
explanation.walkthrough: The O sits in the middle of MAN as an empty stomach would.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means making a low mournful sound, much as whimpering is.

clue.text: One having a dozen donuts? That's a lot, even for Brits these days!

definitions.text: One having a dozen donuts? That's a lot, even for Brits these days!

parts.note: donuts are ring-shaped like the digit 0: a one with twelve of them after it

parts.words: That's a lot, even for Brits these days!
parts.note: the UK used a long scale for big numbers until 1974 and now uses the shorter US one

explanation.surface: Someone eating twelve donuts is told that's a lot even by British standards.
explanation.walkthrough: The donuts are zeros. 'These days' is fair: the older British trillion had eighteen zeros, a million million million, not twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Written out it is 1,000,000,000,000: a one followed by twelve noughts.

clue.text: Long robes from C&A worn over short stockings

parts.note: C&A's: C&A was a British high-street clothes shop

explanation.surface: Clothes shopping: long robes bought at C&A, worn over socks.
explanation.walkthrough: C&A was a cheap clothing chain found on every British high street until 2001.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy and choristers wear these ankle-length garments, the classic long robe of the church.

clue.text: Permission to depart for holiday

definitions.meaning: what a soldier or pupil asks for before going
time off work, as in annual or maternity

explanation.surface: An employee asks permission to go on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses sit in the same office scene, which is why the join is hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday English: a soldier asks it to go, and an employee takes it annually as a holiday.

clue.text: Fake Tales of San Francisco echo in song. Alex Turner originally arranged …

indicators.note: 'originally' as at the origin: take each word's first letter
music is arranged, and so are letters, into a new order

parts.words: Francisco echo in song. Alex Turner
parts.note: first letters of Francisco, echo, in, song, Alex, Turner

explanation.surface: Liner notes: the Arctic Monkeys song Fake Tales of San Francisco, arranged by frontman Alex Turner.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title is split: its first two words are the definition and SAN goes into the fodder. The ellipsis runs this clue on into 11 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fantasy is an imagined story, so these are tales that are fake.

clue.text: … Dancing Shoes track and treats …

indicators.note: dancers move around the floor, so the letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: Continuing the Arctic Monkeys list: the track Dancing Shoes, and some treats.
explanation.walkthrough: Dancing Shoes is an Arctic Monkeys song, so 'Dancing' hides as part of a title.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: crumbly sweet cakes, often served with strawberries, are one kind of treat.

clue.text: … high part in vocal tonally

indicators.note: 'in' as location: the answer sits in the following words, across their join

explanation.surface: The end of the song list: a high part sung with good tone.
explanation.walkthrough: The music surface makes ALTO feel like a definition only, but it sits across the join of 'vocal tonally'.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical term: in a choir this line sits above the tenor, and for men it is the highest part.

clue.text: Carry cold and hot tea inside something handy for a seaside picnic

definitions.text: something handy for a seaside picnic

parts.note: C = cold, as on a tap
H = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Packing a flask of hot tea and some cold drinks for a day at the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: The flask of tea belongs to the picnic, which keeps CHAI out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a folding seat you carry down to the sand is one thing handy at a seaside picnic.

clue.text: A Certain Romance is next to be mixed to get disc right

indicators.note: a track is mixed in the studio, and letters mixed come out in a new order

explanation.surface: A DJ's playlist: the Arctic Monkeys song A Certain Romance comes next, remixed onto disc.
explanation.walkthrough: The Arctic Monkeys song title is the definition: the answer is a certain romance, a famous weepie film.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 2004 weepie from Nicholas Sparks's novel is one particular romance, playing on the song title.

clue.text: They may require medicines essentially injected into the skin right away

indicators.note: a word's essence is its heart, so take the central letter
'right away' has R go away, removed from the skin word

parts.note: EPIDERMIS, the skin, with R (right) taken away

indicators.note: 'injected into' as insertion

explanation.surface: An injection of medicine into the skin, given straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as 'at once'; here it is R removed. 'Medicines' works twice, ending the definition and supplying the C.
explanation.definitionFit: Widespread outbreaks of disease call for mass treatment, so they may require medicines.

clue.text: Drunkenly call "I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor" like this

indicators.note: a drunk jumbles his words, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.words: You Look Good on the Dancefloor"
parts.note: rest of the song title: surface only, pointed at by 'like this'

explanation.surface: A drunk bellows the Arctic Monkeys title I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like this' points back at the song title: looking good on the dancefloor is moving like a ballet dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: Graceful and poised as a ballet dancer, which is how the song title imagines you look on the dancefloor.

clue.text: The View from the Afternoon, one's grabbing coat, leaving at the end

indicators.note: 'grabbing' as holding: P...MA takes hold of the coat letters
the coat leaves off its end, losing its last letter

parts.note: ANORAK, a hooded jacket, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: Arctic Monkeys again: the song The View from the Afternoon, and someone grabbing a coat on the way out.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title splits: 'The View' is the definition and 'Afternoon' gives PM. 'Leaving at the end' sounds like a person going; it cuts the K.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: this is an unbroken, sweeping view over a wide area.

clue.text: Like a rebel, Andy Nicholson initially has his go in Arctic …

indicators.note: 'initially' as at the start: the first letters of Andy Nicholson
'go in' as entering: HIS goes in to ARCTIC, between ARC and TIC

parts.note: used whole, opened up to take HIS

explanation.surface: Andy Nicholson, Arctic Monkeys' first bass player, takes his turn in the band, rebel-style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has his go' reads as taking a turn; the wordplay has HIS going into ARCTIC. The ellipsis runs the band name on into 21 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchists reject all authority, so behaving in their manner is behaving like a rebel.

clue.text: To supply a department requires a lot of shipping

parts.note: to arm is to supply with weapons
a, plus d. = department, a dictionary abbreviation
the a of 'a lot', used as printed

explanation.surface: Stocking a store department needs a lot of shipments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shipping' in the surface is sending goods; in the definition it is ships themselves, collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: A great fleet, as with the Spanish one of 1588, is a lot of ships: shipping in the collective sense.

clue.text: Matches at night need them

parts.note: reads as things you strike; here sports fixtures
evening games are played under floodlit towers

explanation.surface: Striking matches in the dark to see by.
explanation.walkthrough: Matches that give light push you towards flames; the matches are football games, played at night under floodlights.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening football and cricket are played under floodlights, which the clue calls simply 'them'.

clue.text: … Monkeys' first appearance. Topping the bill, the gents dominate

indicators.note: a word's first appearance is its first letter

parts.note: the gents is the men's toilet, the loo

explanation.surface: Arctic Monkeys headline their first gig and dominate the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping the bill' sounds like headlining; it puts LOO before M. The gents is British for the men's toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise up large and threatening over something, towering over it, is a way to dominate it.

clue.text: How extremely capable girl's reconnected small woofer

indicators.note: wires reconnected run differently, so the letters are put in a new order
'extremely' as at the extremes: only the first and last letters of capable

explanation.surface: Praise for a clever girl who rewired a small loudspeaker.
explanation.walkthrough: A woofer is the bass speaker in a hi-fi, and also a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful definition: this short-legged breed, beloved of the late Queen, is a small dog, and a dog is a woofer.

clue.text: What centurion used to cover face when wrapped up

indicators.note: something wrapped up is rolled up, and in a down clue rolling up reverses the letters

explanation.surface: A Roman officer hides his face in his cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: A rare word, so the wordplay has to carry it: the surface's cloak is exactly what the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical term: the woollen cloak worn by Roman soldiers, centurions included, to cover themselves.

clue.text: When the Sun Goes Down single's number 1 in this country

indicators.note: number 1 in each word is its first letter: of Down and of single

parts.note: the United Kingdom, where the paper is printed

explanation.surface: When the Sun Goes Down was an Arctic Monkeys number 1 single in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title splits: 'When the Sun Goes' is the definition and 'Down' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The fading light of evening is the time of day when the sun goes down.

clue.text: Dung cart I upset causing smearing

indicators.note: a cart upset is tipped over, so its letters spill out in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tips over a dung cart and gets muck smeared everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smearing' is literal in the surface; the definition is its figurative sense, blackening a reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the figurative sense: to traduce is to slander, and smearing is blackening a name.

clue.text: Norfolk estuary, indefinitely flooded?

indicators.note: grammar's indefinite article is A, so THE is swapped for A

parts.note: the indefinite article, in place of THE
THE WASH, the bay between Norfolk and Lincolnshire

explanation.surface: A guess that a Norfolk estuary is flooded without end.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wash is a large shallow bay on England's east coast; swap its THE for A.
explanation.definitionFit: Covered or overflowing with water, as a flooded place is.

clue.text: Listen! In case it's not finished, they'll produce stuff to feed 21 in India

definitions.text: they'll produce stuff to feed 21 in India

indicators.note: a case not finished is missing its end, so CASE loses its last letter

explanation.surface: An urgent warning to listen in case something is left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 across is LOOM, so the stuff is yarn: the answer is Indian spinning wheels.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: these hand spinning wheels of India make yarn, which is fed to a loom.

clue.text: Is Mardy Bum to make tens of thousands?

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means bad or faulty, so the letters are wrong and need rearranging

explanation.surface: Asking whether the Arctic Monkeys song Mardy Bum will earn a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Mardy Bum is an Arctic Monkeys song; 'mardy' is northern English for sulky, and 'bum' breaks away to be the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictly, from Greek myrias, one is ten thousand, so several make tens of thousands.
